But over to you. Oh my gosh. Now it's not going to... Oh, having a bit of technical difficulty.

Nope. No. This? Yeah. Oh, yes. You can start now. Ka pai. All right. Tēnā tātou katoa. Ki ngā mema o tēnei komiti, tēnā koutou. Ki ngā whānau kāinga kore o Aotearoa, tēnā koutou. Ki a koutou katoa kua kōrerotia ki tēnei pere kino, tēnā koutou katoa.

Kua maumahara tātou i a rātou, ngā whānau kāinga kore, kua whetū rangatira i te wā o Matariki. Kia ū ō moeroa i ngā ringaringa o ō tūpuna. Haere, haere, haere atu rā. Waiho ake rātou ki a rātou, ā, tātou te hunga ora ki a tātou. Ko Danielle Marx tōku ingoa.

He mokopuna tēnei o Te Arawa waka mai Maketū ki Tongariro, Tuparetoa, Fiji Ponga hoki. I'm the Waikato Collective Coordinator for Manaaki Rangatahi, here with our Pou Ārahi, Bianca Jansen. We first want to acknowledge all of our whānau who have been abused in state and faith-based care, as today marks two years since the release of the Whanaketia report.

Our solidarity remains with all survivors, past and present, who shared their stories in hopes of action that we are still waiting to be delivered today. Mm. Manaaki Rangatahi is a national collective of youth housing advocates who aim to prevent and end youth homelessness in Aotearoa. Through our collectives in Kaikohe, Whangārei, Tāmaki Makaurau, Waikato, Hawke's Bay, Pōneke and Ōtautahi, we work in collaboration with service providers to ensure rangatahi are housed and have the necessary wraparound support.

We oppose this bill in its entirety and have concerns particularly around children experiencing homelessness as young as 14 being targeted. This is not the first time Māori have been moved on. Following the signing of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, many tangata whenua have been displaced from their homes. Whether this was from the violence of land wars around the country, or more recent history, forcing our whānau away from their tūrangawaewae to urban centers.

Māori were not homeless peoples. We had abundance in all the ways you can think of. It wasn't until King Tawhiao went to negotiate with the Crown in England that he witnessed homelessness for the first time, not here in Aotearoa, but in England, where this Parliament's history begins. This is a raw reality of being on whenua where horrendous colonial acts of suppression have taken place and continue to this day.

That is the context that must be remembered as this government aims to move children on who have nowhere else to go. Today, this bill continues the colonial legacy of displacement for tangata whenua and many others who call Aotearoa home. We thank all the previous submitters highlighting the fact that children are targeted under this bill.

Our solidarity spans across organizations all around the country, and it is plain to see that no one wants our children to be on the streets, let alone moved on. It's been two years since the Kāinga Kore W2750 report was released, to which we are claimants of. Two years of experience and lived experience highlighting the desperate need for more support, more funding, more care for our homeless whānau.

Yet this government in particular has stripped youth housing providers to bare bones, changed policy that has resulted in declining people's access to MSD support and removed emergency housing. Children do not choose their circumstances. We recognize our takatāpui LGBTQIA+ rangatahi who sometimes choose themselves over bigots and are left to fend for themselves.

We recognize the disabled rangatahi who do not have an accessible house and are left to sleep wherever they can. We recognize the rangatahi moving from house to house through Oranga Tamariki. We recognize rangatahi leaving the criminal justice system with nowhere to go. At the current age this bill targets, 14-year-olds cannot access MSD or many housing services because of the strict nature of contracts, and these are the realities of our young people who are experiencing homelessness in Aotearoa.

We want to speak to the experience of a young person who is currently in transitional housing service in Kerikeri-roa. They were rough sleeping, searching every night for somewhere to sleep, and they would move to another spot the next day to not inconvenience anyone. Those are their words.

Not wanting to be considered an inconvenience. That is the feelings that they were dealing with while trying to find somewhere safe, dry place to rest. They were not harming anyone. The only harm they experienced was the lack of support for suitable housing that could support their needs and aspirations.

They're a strong advocate for youth who are homeless, and I thank them for sharing their story with me to share with you today. Rangatahi in our collective services are fearful of the police. It's obvious why when in Kerikeri-roa, an 11-year-old child was assumed to be an adult mental health patient.

They was then forced into handcuffs and administered antipsychotic medication How many more kids are being assumed older by the police? How many more kids are being targeted by businesses as nuisances, left to be moved on by police who don't really have the capacity to deal with our homeless whanau who just want help?

Children often don't have criminal charges before being homeless. It's the desperation to have a full puku and a good night's rest that drive them to do things that we wouldn't dream of. As we state in our submission, this will create another pipeline to prison, because when you are desperate, you will do anything to survive. And that is not an Aotearoa that we should be proud of.

Once you become labeled by the state as a criminal, you cannot get access to many private and social housing. But everyone deserves a home to go to. Everyone deserves to be treated like a human being, like every single one of you. As this is the Justice Committee, we hope that we can actually see justice for our children who are rough sleeping and begging throughout Aotearoa.

This bill is spending energy on something that won't work. Our collective knows the answers to youth homelessness and has been delivering positive outcomes. This parliament could support the Honorable Marama Davidson's bill, ensuring that no child is exited out of Oranga Tamariki without a house and financial support. It could support or any Kai Parata members bill that will cut to the core of why our rangatahi are homeless.

We want real solutions to the catastrophe that is youth homelessness in Aotearoa, and we actually needed them yesterday. It would have been amazing if these move on orders were moving people into long-term housing solutions with wraparound support, but then we wouldn't be here today. While we cannot trust that this bill will be thrown out, we implore you to do the bare minimum and raise the age from 14 to 18.

Our children deserve to be treated with dignity and respect. House our children. Don't criminalize them and push them further into the margins. Mm. Adorn the bird with feathers so that they may fly. Adorn our rangatahi with housing. Adorn our rangatahi with an opportunity to thrive so that they can dream and be the people they want to see in Aotearoa, in this ao.

Thank you, Danielle. We've got a couple of questions from some members. We're going to start with Dan Rose warm. Yeah. Thanks, Danielle Bianca, for that submission. It highlights that this bill creates another pathway into the justice system for young people who are already experiencing homelessness. And drawing from your experience, I was just wondering if you could explain to the committee how a homeless young person could move from needing support to becoming involved with the criminal justice system under this bill.

Well, the system is incredibly broken as it currently is. So if you're a rangatahi tonight, in Aotearoa that's facing housing insecurity and homelessness, you will find it nearly impossible to find anywhere for yourself. There isn't front-facing information on how to get into immediate access or emergency housing.

The system is very complex to navigate. If you contact MSD, you're going to barely make it to the receptionist, let alone actually be seen and housed, and you are advocating for that all by yourself. So MSD has a system where if you go into MSD, you then have to go from there to a youth payment provider.

So let's take, for example, MSD Queen Street. The nearest youth payment provider is Youthline in Epsom. You have to get there by yourself as a young person, usually with no money, no HOP card, no ID, and no way of navigating yourself there. So how rangatahi fall into the justice system is because they are falling down all of the gaps that we as Aotearoa are giving to our rangatahi when they are faced with houselessness and homelessness.

And we had a rangatahi that we were working with that was sleeping at the train station in Manukau, and he was going to join a gang so that he could get housing and somewhere to sleep. So if that's not a pipeline into getting involved with criminal activity and actually going to somewhere where you know within your own connection and systems that you can get some support. If the gangs are the only place that our rangatahi can go to to get support, we are incredibly broken as a country. That is just absolutely abhorrent and our rangatahi deserve better.

And that's not just rangatahi Maori, that's rangatahi that find themselves on the streets. Thank you. We've got time for one more quick question from Todd Stevens. Oh, thank you. Thank you for being here and your advocacy, and your points are well made, and obviously the age is something that people- Mm. I just had more of a just curiosity question. You and the services you represent, what's the youngest people you're now seeing on the street homeless, and has that changed in the last decade?

It's changed since this incumbent government has been in, and it also has changed since I've been in Manaaki Rangatahi, and I've been a social worker for 30 years, near on 30 years, and definitely there are a lot younger people. We've been told by the Pride Project, who are based out in Manurewa, that they are picking up and talking to around 10 to 12-year-olds that are sitting in bus stops with nowhere to go and have taken off from home because home is a violent, unsafe space for them.

And there isn't anyone picking up a lot of those young people. So we really need to listen to our communities when it comes to the solutions for rangatahi because our Community providers are seeing what's on the ground, and they can offer solutions. Thank you very much. Thank you, Danielle and Bianca, for joining us this afternoon.
Kia ora. Thank you. Thank you. Right. Our next submitter is the Wellington City Mission. Murray, Pip, and Maria, if you can come up, please.

Good afternoon. Thank you for joining us. We've got you down for 10 minutes. We've read your written submission. Just leave some time at the end for questions. But over to you. Thank you. And kia ora koutou. Thank you for the opportunity to present today. I'm Murray Edwards, the Wellington City Missioner, joined by two of my assistant city missioner colleagues, Maria Millen- Kia ora... and Pip Rae, and also have with me my board chair, John Morris, and some of the whānau from the Wellington City Mission.

The Wellington City Mission has served the communities of the greater Wellington region for 122 years now, and our role is to support those who are struggling the most. In recent years, this has increasingly been in response to issues of poverty, a lack of wellbeing, and homelessness.

This makes us, alongside our colleagues and our colleague agencies, the front line in response to the issues of social and economic deprivation that have been talked about extensively throughout your select committee process. Every day, we see those who are suffering from homelessness, mental health challenges, addictions, loss of connection with whānau and friends, and an inability to obtain and retain meaningful employment, and many more such issues.

Our lives are interwoven with theirs, and often we have the honor of being invited into the intimacy of their lives and their circumstances. Given that, I want to pose the question that we concluded our written submission with: What do we do with the privilege we have?

The privilege that you have, that I have, that we have. The privilege that so often we take for granted and assume is available to everyone. That is not how it is for many people. So the question today is what are you going to do as members of this committee with the privilege you have?

Can I commend you on the way you've conducted your hearings over the last two weeks? I've watched and listened to most of the submissions. It's not an easy task you have. I don't envy your job. But I have to acknowledge, throughout it all, you've been generous and compassionate to every single person you've engaged with, irrespective of the views they might have expressed or how they might have expressed them.

One of our key objectives in the Wellington City Mission is to build a community where there is no us and them. What that means in our service delivery is that we treat every person with dignity and with respect and without judgment, irrespective of their circumstances. I believe that you've done that throughout this select committee process.

Thank you. And now I ask you to apply those same principles to how we treat people in our community that need the most help. The Wellington City Mission is one of the largest social housing and community service providers in the Wellington region, and one of the very few that operates 24/7, 365 days a year.

By definition, therefore, the move on destination for many of the people who may be impacted by this legislation in Wellington is us. Let me tell you today that despite our size and capability, we are full to overflowing. If we weren't so, there wouldn't be so many people on the streets of Wellington.

Our services are bursting at the seams, as are most of the services of the community agencies throughout this country. The myth being postulated by proponents of this bill is that there's a move on to somewhere better. But that is in fact a myth. The Cabinet decision that initiated this legislative proposal was entitled Strengthening Responses to Public Disorder.

That's a laudable objective and worthy of a government that's acting in the best interests of its whole constituency. The sole issue for us in this proposal is the intention to extend the powers that are being imposed on the police to apply to those that aren't contributing to public disorder but are just trying to survive.

I've listened to the Honorable Paul Goldsmith's public commentary on move on orders since he announced the legislation in February of this year. Despite being repeatedly questioned about the application of move on orders to those rough sleeping and begging, he consistently ignores the question and refers to disorderly behavior in public places and the need to reclaim our city streets.

None of the minister's commentary justifies why those who are required to sleep rough and to beg just to survive are captured by this legal intention. Unless maybe we just don't want to see them there. In considering this bill, you must make the critical distinction between circumstance and behaviors.

Behaviors that disrupt, threaten, or offend should be responded to. But surely the only consequence of those sleeping rough or begging is shame and embarrassment. Not for them, but for me, and for you, and for all of us. I feel ashamed when some in our community have no legitimate or safe alternative to sleeping rough.

You should too. I believe those circumstances to be our failure, not theirs. I note in the written submission that the government of the United United Kingdom on Monday, the 29th of June, repealed the 202-year-old Vagrancy Act that criminalized those sleeping rough. And I note now that the new UK Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said on Monday, and I quote, "On my first day as Prime Minister, I'm announcing this government's commitment to finally end long-term rough sleeping across the UK at the earliest opportunity.

We will get to work immediately, bringing together national and local government with the investment needed to get it done." Investment of over 3.8 billion pounds over the next three years. The country's leadership in the United Kingdom is doing something about this highly complex issue. Our political direction seems to be heading in the other way.

As I conclude my comments, I want to say that I believe this is a critical moment in our New Zealand history. And I don't want to be melodramatic about that, but are we going to be a country that ignores, discards, and seeks to hide away those that are struggling the most? Or are we going to be the New Zealand that we always thought we were and aspired to be? If you, as a committee, recommend to Parliament this bill proceeds into law, you need to demonstrate the political and moral leadership New Zealand requires of you. To do that, you need to delete

Section 8, Subsections E and F. We ask you to please remove the inclusion of rough sleeping and begging from this bill. Thank you. Thanks, Murray. We've got time for one question, and it's from Camilla Belich. I'm sorry, Celia, we will get to you. Thank you very much, Murray. That was a very articulate, very moving submission, and thanks for all the work that the Wellington City Mission does.

I think you've articulated really well in your written submission and comments around the difference between rough sleeping and homelessness and begging, and the intimidating behavior that the minister says that he wants to prevent. In your view, if those particular sections you asked to remove were removed, in the bill as it stands, would that bill be something that would be acceptable to you?

Or is it more of a fundamental opposition to the- Look, I think the bill is absolutely acceptable with the removal of Subsections E and F. I'm not sure the bill is necessary, but if on the basis of law and order is the motivation, absolutely, that's okay. The extension to E and F is what is problematic in the bill.

Can I add that I think there's some inherent complications in the bill around the age of 14, around some of the definitions of begging. I believe those challenges disappear if you remove the rough sleeping and begging component of the bill. Thank you. Thank you very much for your submission today.

And thank you. There's no further questions. You're welcome. Thank you. In order. We wish you well with your proceeds. Thank you so much. Our next submitter is Save the Children by Zoom. So we'll just wait for Jackie. Is there a- Yes.

Just in the Zoom, the video is not on the screen. It's nice and dark. If you're there as Jackie, if you could put your camera on, please. We're not hearing Hi, how are you? Kia ora. Thank you. Yes, it's Jackie. My camera, mic, and my camera and audio are on. I do see you now. Welcome.

We've read your submission. Please, if you'd like to leave some time for some questions, but we've got five minutes with you today. Thank you. Thank you. Kia ora . Jackie Southey, Te Korowai Ngā, Ngā Waru Rapora Home, the Child Rights Advocacy and Research Director for Save the Children. Save the Children was founded in 1919 and has been working in Aotearoa, New Zealand since 1947, and we focus on advancing the rights of children at all levels, including legislation, policy, and budgeting for children in order to ensure children's rights are

integral to their daily lives. We welcome the opportunity to share our submission on the Summary Offences Move on Orders Amendment Bill. Save the Children does not support the Summary Offences Move on Orders Amendment Bill. We agree that disorderly or frightening behavior should be appropriately addressed, yet we are concerned that the proposed legislation is targeting some of our most vulnerable citizens and will criminalize rather than help or address the serious issues of homelessness and rough sleeping, a lack of income support, and reliance on begging just

to get by. Our concerns related to the proposed amendment to the legislation include begging, including passive begging, could become a criminal offense. Rough sleeping could become a criminal offense. The proposed legislation applies to children aged 14 to 17 years, and Maori will be disproportionately affected given they are already disproportionately affected by homelessness and rough sleeping.

The proposed legislation applies a jail term of up to three months for breaching a move on order. The legislation moves on or pushes the serious and complex problems of begging and homelessness out of sight rather than providing effective solutions, and the legislation is being rushed through without any consultation of frontline providers or people already vulnerable who will be most impacted by this bill.

Ministry of Justice analysis has found that move on orders merely displace begging behavior and rough sleeping behavior rather than addressing or resolving it. And this is particularly relevant to those that are begging, rough sleeping, and creating makeshift dwellings. These are driven by need. This means that move on orders are highly likely to shift these behaviors to different locations rather than resolving them, and are inferior to existing levers for dealing with disorderly behavior by young people, including referring them to Youth Aid.

The applying of fines for non-compliance with a move on order that was issued for begging, rough sleeping, or creating a makeshift dwelling are not effective to these behaviors, and the bill will disproportionately affect Māori, Pacific, young people, disabled people, and people experiencing mental health and distress. Similar to our concerns, we are aware that Auckland councilors have expressed serious concerns about the bill due to the bill's failure to address the drivers of rough sleeping and begging, and that the bill will move these behaviors to other

areas, and people lightly become more at risk as they become separated from support mechanisms that are currently in place to provide help, such as the Auckland City Mission. Frontline responders such as Kickback Make Change, Auckland City Mission, Wellington City Mission, clearly oppose the bill, as do mental health bodies who are united in their opposition.

So move on. Move on to where? There is nowhere to go. Living on the street is a symptom of serious social issues and deprivation that need to be addressed rather than criminalized. Save the Children's deeply worried that this bill is being introduced at a time when homelessness and levels of serious deprivation are increasing.

One in 10 people, or 473,000, are living in poverty. This means they're unable to afford costs of rent, power, food, transport, and healthcare, and are making incredibly tough choices of which one of those they'll be able to pay for. Youth are particularly affected by youth unemployment, and it's at a 10-year high. Current welfare and support systems are failing to provide a safety net for our whānau, our young people, and individuals that need it.

Young people are often invisible in terms of homelessness, as they are unable to access government supports due to their age, lack the experience and support mechanisms required to access employment, and are often driven to homelessness and rough sleeping due to a complete lack of family support networks, or due to being victims of serious crime and abuse. According to Statistics New Zealand, in more than 2023, and we fear it has exacerbated in that time, 112,000 people, or 2.3% of our population, were estimated to be severely housing deprived.

Children are caught up in severe housing deprivation, and we need to act. These statistics are particularly grim, and we urge the government to redirect efforts to meaningfully address these issues by investing in frontline health and social responses needed to support in response rather than criminalize, and also to effectively address the drivers of serious social deprivation that lead to homelessness and begging.

We call on the government to invest in health and social support that will support and uphold the rights of all of our New Zealanders, including some of our most vulnerable children, youth, and adults. It is not acceptable to criminalize those that are most in need of our help and our compassion. That concludes our submission, and I'm happy to take any questions.

Thank you very much, Jackie. We'll just see if there's any questions. Yours from Camilla Belich. Thank you so much, Jackie, and for all the work that Save the Children does. I just wanted to ask you, from your experience dealing with children who this bill may apply to if it was a law, what are their stories? Why do they end up in this situation?

What can you tell us about them? What we know from talking with our partners that work on the frontline is that a key driver of being homeless and being on the streets as a young person is through experiencing abuse and harm, and sadly, it can be in their own homes, and without the ability to deal with it. Harrowing stories by young people who had no place to go were shared at the final Child Poverty Monitor launch that was held at Waitematā in Auckland, I think around three years ago.

And we need to be able to address those drivers. We cannot criminalize these young people who simply have nowhere to go. We also know that those frontline providers are struggling with funding and capability to address the need. And we know from people that reach out and community stories, and stories feels like the wrong word because it's their lives and it's their experiences, that the ability to afford private rental houses is very, very hard, and that is pushing regular ... well, families that we should be able to house, that are

not beset by addiction and issues, into homelessness. So it's not limited to people who have addiction and those other sort of issues that we sort of see at the frontline of homelessness. It is increasingly people who really just cannot afford to make ends meet. Thank you. Thank you, Jackie. We don't have any further questions, so thank you very much for your submission.

Thank you, Kelda. Thank you. Next is in person, Reverend Brett Reed and Leanne Munro. If they're here, thank you. Please come forward. Welcome. We've got you for 10 minutes. Your submission has been read, and if you want to just leave some time for some questions, we're in your hands. Thank you.

Sure. Great. Tuhiia ki te rangi. Tuhiia ki te whenua. Tuhiia ki te ngākau o ngā tāngata katoa. Ko te mea nui, ko te aroha. E mihi ana ahau ki Te Atua. Nāna nei ngā mea katoa. E ngā Mema Pāremata, tēnā koutou katoa. Me nga kaiwhakapuoro hoki, tena koutou katoa. Greetings to you all, and thank you for this opportunity for us to present today.

My name is Brett Reed. I'm the Minister of Ngaio Union Church, a church in Wellington. I'm joined by the Reverend Leanne Munro, a member of our congregation, and we're presenting this submission on behalf of Ngaio Union Church. As a faith community committed to the way of Jesus, we are guided by the values of compassion, love of neighbor, and care for those in need.

It is because of these values that we oppose the proposed move on orders. We all want safe and welcoming public spaces, but homelessness is not solved by moving people from one place to another. The proposed measures simply displace people from places and communities they rely on, while leaving the underlying need for housing and support unchanged.

In many cases, simply moving people on will make it even harder for them to access the help they need. Over the past week and a bit, you've heard from experts in the field, and we tautoko what they have already said. In our written submission, we speak about a longtime association with DCM in Wellington.

Through their work, we know that the claim that rough sleepers have somewhere to move on to is simply untrue, and Murray Edridge touched on this as well. In the last quarter alone, DCM supported 150 people with no house or shelter to go to, and they continue to support dozens of people sleeping rough because there is nowhere else for them to live.

Homelessness is a complex issue with housing, health, and social causes. The people affected are often living with poverty, mental ill health, addiction, or multiple challenges at once. These are issues that require coordinated, evidence-based support, not punitive measures. And I'll hand over to Leanne.

Tena koutou katoa. I'm speaking as a person who somewhat imperfectly tries to live out her faith every day. The biblical gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke each tell of an occasion where Jesus of Nazareth was engaged in conversation and asked a simple question, "Which command is the greatest?"

His response is taken directly from the Hebrew scriptures he knew, the Torah. "Love God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength, and love your neighbor as you love yourself." In the Gospel of Luke, in response to a further, some would say, smartarsed question, but the jury is out on that, he is asked, "But who is my neighbor?"

And he responds with a story that many of us have come to know as the story of the Good Samaritan. In effect, Jesus says, "Your neighbor is the one you see as different to yourself, and not in a good way." Last year, walking down Willis Street to the bank, I noticed two different people in separate locations sitting on the pavement outside the buildings.

Each had a card seeking help from passersby. I didn't stop. I was in a hurry to get to my meeting. Afterwards, though, I approached the woman and greeted her, receiving a very gracious response, and said I was going to get a cuppa and would she like one. It was one of Wellington's lovely sunny but slightly cool days.

She was surprised but thanked me and said yes, and on my return, when I offered her a piece of banana loaf I'd also purchased, she declined graciously, saying the cup of tea was enough, and I felt incredibly humbled. Mm. We talked for another minute or so, and I asked if she knew about DCM and the City Mission, and she replied yes, and then we said goodbye and she wished me a good day.

Further up the road, a youngish man I'd seen appeared to be talking to himself. Somewhat in trepidation, I approached him and greeted him, saying my name, getting an enthusiastic, "Kia ora," in response. I offered him the piece of loaf, to which he replied, "Oh, are you sure, ma'am?"

Now, I may be nearly 64, and I may have silver hair, but I'm still not used to being called ma'am. As we parted company, he also graciously wished me a good day. I was struck by their dignity, their cautious friendliness, and the graciousness of their responses.

I was also aware as I spoke with them of the sidelong looks we got from our fellow Wellingtonians who continued to pass by, as if it was odd for two people to share conversation on a public street. And I felt a sense of shame that these two fellow Wellingtonians were having to do this, for whatever reason.

There is no simple solution to the homelessness, the rough sleeping, the begging that we see. But it appears that this is what this proposed law change seeks to be. But we are talking about fellow human beings, people like you and I, who are different perhaps, and who for a variety of reasons have ended up where they are Because I am commanded to love my neighbor as myself, I can do no other than oppose this proposed law

change and ask that you, as our elected representatives, show mercy and compassion to those that this law, perhaps unintentionally, I hope so, seeks to put out of sight, out of mind. Instead of move on orders, we urge the government to invest in what we know works. More social and affordable housing, stronger health and addiction services, and outreach programs.

Justice is not about punishing people for having nowhere to go. It's about restoring dignity, providing support, and addressing the causes of homelessness. For these reasons, we urge you to reject the proposed legislation and invest instead in evidence-based responses that we know work.

Thank you very much, Brett and Leanne. A very heartfelt submission. We do have a question from Camilla Belich. Thank you both for your submission. It was very moving. I have to say, a number of the faith organizations who have submitted to the committee made very compelling and moving submissions.

I had a question around what you were discussing, Leanne, around the almost hesitation that some of the homeless community may have when interacting with other people, members of the public, people trying to help, presumably people in positions of authority as well. Do you think that if the people that you were engaging with, if they had been moved on and had been in a different place, do you think that would've affected the way that they interacted? Or what would the psychological impact of what this bill has proposed, in terms of

their attitude towards people engaging with them be? You're probably better to ask someone like Murray that question, who has direct everyday contact, or the workers at both DCM and Wellington City Mission. I don't know. Maybe you could ask the people themselves how that would impact them.

Yeah. Well, we've got Auckland City Mission coming up, so- Maybe you could ask the people who this will affect directly the question. Yeah. Thank you. If we have time. Yes. Thank you. Look, thank you. And I'm really loving all the teaching everyone about some Christian values. It's beautiful. It's not usual here.

But I just want to ask, when we apply compassion for our neighbors, what about those that are trying to run a business to provide some kai for their families, and that are really struggling to get patrons, as I've been told in South Auckland, because of our poor homeless people, and I understand they're in rough spaces, but that are congregating in front of their shops and other people, not you and I, but other people, are too intimidated to go in.

And they're going to have to get two jobs, other jobs, because they're losing patrons. Yeah, sure. Where is the compassion for them? I think to say that there's any kind of one overarching response to anything is maybe a little simplistic. So, to suggest that this is going to be helpful for everyone is near impossible.

From our perspective, having compassion is understanding where people are coming from. Yeah. And we have compassion for all people, for folk who are trying to run businesses as well as the homeless and people who are begging.
